title: Brotherhood
sourceDocTitle: CHOSEN: THE STORY BEFORE THE MANGER-SCRIPT
publicationNote: This scene was auto-published from the CHOSEN master script.

blocks.text: Characters: JOSEPH, LEVI, MALACHI, CALEB, EZRA, MARY, SHIRA
Scene 4 ends somewhere else in Nazareth with the dangerous echo: 'That's what I heard.'
Lights cut to Joseph's work area. The tonal shift should be immediate: warmth, laughter, physical energy.
JOSEPH, LEVI, MALACHI, CALEB, and EZRA are already working together. The unfinished table from Scene 2 is now unmistakably the project.
The satchel Mary made Joseph is on him. Do not feature it yet.
JOSEPH, LEVI, MALACHI, CALEB and EZRA are already working.
They do not stand in a line.
wood passes from hand to hand;
someone catches something at the last second.
These men have worked together for years.
Do not begin with dialogue. Let the audience watch the men work.
Joseph checks a length. Levi takes weight. Ezra checks alignment. Malachi steadies a piece. Caleb tries to help and is just useful enough to remain employed.
The physical vocabulary beneath the sequence is MEASURE -> MARK -> CUT -> SET. It may be expressed through movement rather than repeated as lyrics.
Hammer strikes, scraping wood, footwork, hand-claps, and safe prop percussion begin to align into a musical pulse.
That is a form of holding.
They keep working. The rhythm continues underneath.
Joseph stops and looks at a piece Caleb has handled.
Only if you compare it to the other side.
Joseph takes the piece from Caleb.
The men laugh. Joseph resets the piece, and the music/movement picks back up.
Levi notices Joseph working on another piece.
Ezra watches Joseph inspect the table.
And you've checked that corner four times.
Man hasn't even married her, and he's already building furniture.
At least he'll have somewhere to sleep after she gets tired of him.
This one appears to be a table.
This time he answers without joking.
That quiets them for just a moment.
Caleb grabs the appropriate piece and launches back into the work.
The men laugh and return to the work rhythm. Joseph tries to hide how pleased he is, which only confirms everything.
Caleb reaches for a tool and notices Joseph's satchel.
The others notice the satchel is nearly empty.
She made you a satchel, and now you're protecting it from the tools.
Joseph looks at all of them.
Joseph throws a rag at Caleb. Caleb catches it triumphantly.
The carpentry pulse now expands into the full Brotherhood sequence.

This should feel rehearsed and exciting, but never disconnected from the work. The men are not presenting choreography to the audience; they are working so instinctively together that the work becomes choreography.

Movement possibilities: passing wood in counter-rhythm; coordinated lifts; safe tool-handling phrases; turns generated by carrying material; foot-stomps; hand-claps; bench/wood percussion; a repeated lift-set-release pattern; Caleb adding unnecessary flourishes that the others repeatedly correct.
Joseph should eventually stop supervising every beat and fully join the physical joy. We need to see him young, competitive, laughing and completely at home with these men.
The men begin passing tools in rhythm.
The dialogue starts locking into tempo.
I was going to say share it.
And if the plan goes bad—
This portion may become sung/spoken/rap-adjacent depending on Christian's composition.
The text can ultimately be shaped musically, but the dramatic territory is
When one man loses his footing—
When one man misses the measure—
The phrase should land clearly enough to return emotionally later.
The music expands into approximately 20–30 seconds of instrumental choreography.
This is the major visual payoff of the scene.
jumps over low work pieces where safe;
five-man formations that constantly break and reform.
The choreography should feel as though construction itself has become dance.
One man throws a lightweight piece of wood.
Laughter. Breath. The men remain in the world of the workshop rather than posing for applause.
That is how you build a table.
You were the reason morale was necessary.
Joseph looks at the table. He is pleased despite himself.
Joseph looks toward the table again, then unconsciously touches or adjusts the satchel.
The man is getting married, building a table for half of Nazareth, and all we get is 'good.'
That lands. Joseph does not need a speech.
The others see that he means it.
Then remember us when you become respectable.
Exactly. Someone has to protect you from it.
Assuming Caleb does not improve anything overnight.
When real trouble comes, you'll know the difference.
When trouble comes, we stand together.
The line should not become solemn. It is simply true to Joseph in this moment.
Caleb looks at Ezra and shakes his head. They laugh again.
The men move back into the work.
The rhythm begins again—easy now. Familiar.
At the edge of the space, MARY appears.
Mary watches Joseph laughing with his friends.
The satchel she made him still on his shoulder.
For a moment, she almost says yes.
Shira offers her hand. Mary takes it briefly.
Shira moves away but does not need to disappear immediately. Mary is now alone at the edge of Joseph's world.
I'm just saying, eight chairs is a commitment.
You are standing next to him.
Behind Joseph, the work begins to stop.
Joseph gives him the smallest nod: I've got it.
The men begin putting down and gathering their tools.
Levi starts to leave, then turns back.
Malachi lingers for only a moment.
The rhythm that filled the room is gone.
Shira looks once more toward Mary.
Mary gives her a small nod.
The satchel Mary made is still on Joseph.
Everything Joseph believes his future will be is physically present around him.
He sets down the tool in his hand.
I need to tell you something.

The biggest theatrical opportunity here is that the scene has two completely different endings at once: musically, “Brotherhood” can earn a genuine applause button; dramatically, the applause is followed almost immediately by Mary appearing while Joseph is still glowing from everything he thinks his future will be. That contrast should make the audience uneasy even while they are enjoying the number.

I would also have Mickey preserve a very recognizable five-beat carpentry motif from this scene—something like hammer / hammer / scrape / clap / stomp. Later, after Mary tells Joseph the truth, he can try to work and repeat that exact rhythm

The audience will understand before Joseph says anything: his world no longer fits together. That possibility is explicitly planted in the Scene 5 architecture and is one of the strongest musical-storytelling opportunities in this section.
